name: Augusto Pinochet
description: Chilean ruler assessed through authoritarian political control, market reforms and selective retention of state assets.

axes.brief: Military overthrow, suspended competitive politics and concentration of executive authority defined his rule.
axes.counter: The 1988 plebiscite defeat eventually led to transition; this does not make his preceding rule an ordinary competitive electoral democracy. Expert and union selection are distinct from military command.

axes.brief: Secret police, political detention, censorship and coercive control sharply constrained personal and political liberties.
axes.counter: Some private economic choices and nonpolitical activity were allowed; liberty on an economic axis must not substitute for civil-rights evidence.

axes.brief: A unitary Chilean national identity and assimilation of Indigenous land institutions were promoted.
axes.counter: National ceremonies and Catholic culture do not demonstrate a personal position on each contemporary migrant practice; broad estimates remain qualified.

axes.brief: Security control and managed entry imply tighter settlement conditions and selective openness.
axes.counter: Exile of opponents is not ordinary immigration policy; no direct modern annual housing-linked quota record is established.

axes.brief: Military strength, coercive security and strategic deterrence were prioritised.
axes.counter: The Beagle conflict was ultimately resolved through mediation rather than full war; militarism must not erase that diplomatic qualification.

axes.brief: National sovereignty and rejection of outside political constraints coexisted with economic openness.
axes.counter: Foreign investment and trade liberalisation are not supranational legal authority or a political federation.

axes.brief: Extensive privatisation and private pensions transferred many assets to private owners.
axes.counter: CODELCO remained state-owned and the 1982 crisis brought bank intervention; strategic and emergency public ownership qualify an all-private estimate.

axes.brief: Tariff reduction and trade liberalisation exposed domestic firms to international competition.
axes.counter: The 1982 crisis brought temporary tariff increases and strategic controls; market reforms were not uniformly open at every moment.

axes.brief: Market prices and private allocation replaced much central planning.
axes.counter: Monetary interventions, bank rescues and selective subsidies remained; opposition to unions does not mean wages were freely negotiated on equal terms.

axes.brief: Targeted safety nets, privatised pensions and reduced egalitarian redistribution accompanied market reforms.
axes.counter: Some public support and progressive tax structure remained; this is a programme estimate, not a moral assessment or claim that poverty policy disappeared.

axes.brief: Public Catholic identity and conservative institutions gave religion a ceremonial role.
axes.counter: Civil/military rulers retained policymaking; the Catholic Church also opposed repression, and no general clerical legislative veto is established.

axes.brief: Conservative family and moral customs were protected, with restrictive sexuality and public-expression policies.
axes.counter: Women’s work and private business participation persisted; social tradition must not be treated as evidence of biological causation.

axes.brief: Modernisation, private investment and infrastructure were prioritised.
axes.counter: Technocratic economic reform does not settle speculative enhancement technology; safety-sensitive estimates are deliberately restrained.

axes.brief: A centralised military executive and appointed local authorities constrained regional autonomy.
axes.counter: Administrative decentralisation and municipal service delivery did not confer democratic regional constitutional or secession rights.

axes.brief: The sources concern institutions and public policy, with little exact evidence on comparative human heredity.
axes.counter: These weak estimates draw only on schooling, discipline and modernisation as learned influences; repression, Catholicism and market policies are not genetic theories.
